title: Radiation of Heat
short_intro: Radiation of heat is the mode of heat transfer via electromagnetic waves, primarily in the infrared spectrum, requiring no material medium for propagation. All bodies above absolute zero emit thermal radiation due to thermal agitation of charged particles.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Basic definitions of emissive power, absorptive power, black body radiation, Prevost's theory of heat exchange, Stefan-Boltzmann law, and simple greenhouse effect applications.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Advanced treatments of Planck's radiation law, Wien's displacement law, Rayleigh-Jeans law, Newton's law of cooling calculus derivations, and spectral distribution curves.

prerequisites: Concept of Temperature and Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics
Degrees of Freedom and Law of Equipartition of Energy

concept_notes.heading: Prevost's Theory of Heat Exchange
bullets: Every body at a temperature above absolute zero (0 K) emits thermal radiation to its surroundings and simultaneously absorbs radiation from them.
A body cools when its rate of emission exceeds its rate of absorption, and warms when absorption exceeds emission.
In thermal equilibrium, the rate of emission equals the rate of absorption.

concept_notes.heading: Thermal Radiations and Their Properties
bullets: Thermal radiations are electromagnetic waves belonging to the infrared and visible regions of the spectrum, travelling with the speed of light (c = 3 x 10<sup>8</sup> m/s in vacuum).
They obey the inverse square law of intensity and exhibit phenomena of reflection, refraction, interference, diffraction, and polarization.
Unlike conduction and convection, radiation requires no intervening medium and passes readily through a vacuum.

concept_notes.heading: Emissive Power and Absorptive Power
bullets: Radiant emissive power (E) of a surface is defined as the total amount of radiant energy emitted per unit time per unit surface area for a specific wavelength interval.
Absorptive power (a) or absorptivity is the ratio of the radiant energy absorbed by a body to the total radiant energy incident upon it.
A perfectly black body has an absorptivity of exactly 1 for all incident wavelengths and angles.

concept_notes.heading: Kirchhoff's Law of Radiation
bullets: At any given temperature, the ratio of the emissive power (E) to the absorptive power (a) for a particular wavelength is a constant for all bodies and is equal to the emissive power of a perfectly black body at that same temperature.
Expressed mathematically as E/a = E<sub>b</sub>, implying that good absorbers are good emitters.
Explains Fraunhofer lines in the solar spectrum, where cooler outer vapors of the sun absorb specific wavelengths emitted by the hot inner core.

derivations.title: Stefan-Boltzmann Law and Net Radiation Heat Transfer
derivations.conditions: Black body in an environment at constant absolute temperature
steps: The total radiant energy emitted per second per unit area by a black body is directly proportional to the fourth power of its absolute temperature T: E = \sigma T^{4}
If a black body of surface area A at temperature T is placed in an enclosure at temperature T<sub>0</sub>, it emits energy at a rate Q<sub>emit</sub> = \sigma A T^{4}
Simultaneously, the body absorbs radiant energy from the enclosure at a rate Q<sub>abs</sub> = \sigma A T_{0}^{4}
The net rate of heat loss by radiation is given by subtracting absorption from emission: Q_{net} = \sigma A (T^{4} - T_{0}^{4})

derivations.title: Newton's Law of Cooling from Stefan-Boltzmann Law
derivations.conditions: Small temperature difference between the body and surroundings ((T - T_{0}) \ll T_{0})
steps: Start with the net rate of heat loss from Stefan-Boltzmann law: - \frac{dQ}{dt} = \sigma A e (T^{4} - T_{0}^{4}), where e is emissivity.
Substitute T \approx T_{0} for the terms other than (T - T_{0}): T^{4} - T_{0}^{4} \approx (T - T_{0})(2T_{0})(2T_{0}^{2}) = 4T_{0}^{3}(T - T_{0}).
Substitute this approximation back into the rate equation and write dQ = mc dT to obtain \frac{dT}{dt} = - \frac{4\sigma A e T_{0}^{3}}{mc}(T - T_{0}) = - K(T - T_{0}).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Blackbody Spectral Radiance (Planck's Distribution Curves)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Curves of spectral emissive power E_{\lambda} versus wavelength \lambda for various absolute temperatures T, showing asymmetric peaks that shift to shorter wavelengths as temperature increases.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The area under each curve represents total emissive power \sigma T^{4}. The peak shifts toward shorter wavelengths with rising temperature, illustrating Wien's displacement law.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Directly tested in questions regarding shifts in peak wavelength and verification of Stefan-Boltzmann law integration.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Newton's Law of Cooling Experimental Verification Curve
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A semi-log plot of ln(T - T_{0}) versus time t, yielding a straight line with a negative slope equal to -K.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Linearity of the semi-log plot confirms the exponential decay nature of Newton's law of cooling.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Interpreting experimental gradient to find cooling constant K for a calorimeter.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Ferry's Black Body Apparatus
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A schematic double-walled hollow sphere with a small aperture and an internal conical projection opposite the aperture.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Any radiation entering through the aperture undergoes multiple internal reflections, with a negligible fraction escaping, achieving an effective absorptivity close to 1.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual questions on the practical realization of a perfectly black body.

solved_numericals.question: A metal sphere of radius 0.1 m is heated to 500 K and placed in an environment at 300 K. Assuming it behaves as a black body, calculate the net rate of heat loss by radiation. (Stefan-Boltzmann constant \sigma = 5.67 \times 10^{-8} W m^{-2} K^{-4})
solution_steps: Determine the surface area of the sphere: A = 4 \pi r^{2} = 4 \times \pi \times (0.1)^{2} = 0.04 \pi \approx 0.12566 m^{2}.
Apply the net radiation formula: Q_{net} = \sigma A (T^{4} - T_{0}^{4}).

solved_numericals.question: The spectral emissive power of a black body peaks at a wavelength of \lambda_{m} = 500 nm at a certain temperature T_{1}. If the temperature is increased such that the peak wavelength shifts to 400 nm, find the percentage change in the total emissive power of the black body.
solution_steps: Use Wien's displacement law to find the new temperature T_{2}: \lambda_{1} T_{1} = \lambda_{2} T_{2} \implies 500 T_{1} = 400 T_{2} \implies T_{2} = \frac{5}{4} T_{1} = 1.25 T_{1}.
The total emissive power is proportional to T^{4}: E_{1} = \sigma T_{1}^{4} and E_{2} = \sigma T_{2}^{4} = \sigma (1.25 T_{1})^{4} = 2.4414 \sigma T_{1}^{4}.

solved_numericals.question: A body cools from 80°C to 64°C in 5 minutes in a room maintained at 24°C. Find the time taken by the body to cool from 64°C to 52°C, assuming Newton's law of cooling holds.
solution_steps: Find the average temperature for the first interval: T_{avg1} = \frac{80 + 64}{2} = 72°C.

Apply Newton's law of cooling differential form: \frac{T_{1} - T_{2}}{t} = K(T_{avg} - T_{0}) \implies \frac{80 - 64}{5} = K(72 - 24) \implies \frac{16}{5} = K(48) \implies K = \frac{16}{5 \times 48} = \frac{1}{15} min^{-1}.
Find the average temperature for the second interval: T_{avg2} = \frac{64 + 52}{2} = 58°C.
Apply the equation for the second interval: \frac{64 - 52}{t'} = K(58 - 24) \implies \frac{12}{t'} = \frac{1}{15} (34) \implies t' = \frac{12 \times 15}{34} = \frac{180}{34} \approx 5.29 min.

assumptions_and_limitations: Stefan-Boltzmann law strictly applies only to ideal black bodies; real grey bodies require an emissivity multiplier e.
Newton's law of cooling is an approximation valid only for small temperature differences ((T - T_{0}) \ll T_{0}) where heat loss by conduction and convection is linear with temperature.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Radiation of heat requires air or a material medium to travel from one place to another.
common_misconceptions.correct: Thermal radiation consists of electromagnetic waves and propagates perfectly through a vacuum.
common_misconceptions.why: Confusion with conduction and convection mechanisms which necessitate particle collisions or bulk fluid motion.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A body at room temperature does not emit any thermal radiation because it feels cold to the touch.
common_misconceptions.correct: All bodies above 0 K emit thermal radiation continuously.
common_misconceptions.why: Net emission determines cooling or warming; a body at room temperature emits radiation while simultaneously absorbing radiation from its surroundings.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Newton's law of cooling applies for any arbitrary temperature difference between a body and its surroundings.
common_misconceptions.correct: Newton's law is valid only for small temperature differences (typically < 35°C to 40°C in air).
common_misconceptions.why: For large temperature differences, radiation heat loss follows the fourth-power Stefan-Boltzmann relation rather than a linear temperature difference.

quick_revision: Thermal radiation travels at the speed of light in a vacuum as electromagnetic waves.
A perfect black body has absorptivity a = 1 and emits maximum radiation at any temperature.
Kirchhoff's law states that good absorbers are good emitters at thermal equilibrium (E/a = E_{b}).
Stefan-Boltzmann law gives total emissive power proportional to T^{4}.
Wien's displacement law establishes that \lambda_{m}T = constant, meaning peak wavelength shifts shorter as temperature rises.
Newton's law of cooling simplifies the Stefan-Boltzmann law for small temperature differences into a linear exponential decay.
